statement: For the surplus $X_t = x + \mu t + \sigma B_t$ driven by a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, with $x, \mu, \sigma > 0$, the [ruin probability](c:ruin-probability) is $P(\tau < \infty) = e^{-2\mu x/\sigma^2}$, where $\tau$ is the first zero of $X$.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B_0 = 0$.
The initial capital $x$, the drift $\mu$ and the volatility $\sigma$ are strictly positive constants.

conclusion: $P(\tau < \infty) = \exp(-2\mu x/\sigma^2)$, where $\tau = \inf\{t \ge 0 : X_t = 0\}$.

proofs.name: Exponential martingale and optional stopping
proofs.slogan: The exponential martingale $e^{-\theta(X_t - x)}$ with $\theta = 2\mu/\sigma^2$ is bounded up to ruin, and its limit is $e^{\theta x}$ on ruin and 0 otherwise.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for positive $x$, $\mu$ and $\sigma$. The case $\mu \le 0$, where ruin is certain, is excluded.

roles.why: Independent Gaussian increments make the exponential process a [martingale](c:martingale) and give the law of large numbers for $B$.
$x > 0$ starts the surplus above 0 and bounds the stopped martingale, and $\mu > 0$ makes the surplus tend to $+\infty$ when ruin never occurs.

steps.slogan: Turn the surplus into the [martingale](c:martingale) $M_t = e^{-\theta(X_t - x)}$ with $\theta = 2\mu/\sigma^2$.
steps.detail: The Gaussian increments give $\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda(B_t - B_s)} \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = e^{\lambda^2(t-s)/2}$, so $e^{\lambda B_t - \lambda^2 t/2}$ is a martingale. With $\lambda = -\theta\sigma$ the compensator $\theta^2\sigma^2 t/2 = \theta\mu t$ cancels the drift, so $M_t = e^{-\theta(X_t - x)}$.

steps.slogan: Stop the martingale at the bounded [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $t \wedge \tau$.
steps.detail: Before ruin the surplus is nonnegative, so $0 < M_{t \wedge \tau} \le e^{\theta x}$. Optional stopping at the bounded time $t \wedge \tau$ gives $\mathbb{E} M_{t \wedge \tau} = 1$ for every $t \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $B_t/t \to 0$, so the surplus escapes to infinity when ruin never occurs.
steps.detail: The strong law gives $B_n/n \to 0$. The oscillations $Y_n = \sup_{s \le 1}|B_{n+s} - B_n|$ have $\mathbb{E} Y_n^2 \le 4$ by Doob's inequality, so $\sum_n P(Y_n > \varepsilon n) < \infty$, and Borel-Cantelli gives [almost sure convergence](c:almost-sure-convergence) $B_t/t \to 0$. Hence $X_t \to \infty$ on $\{\tau = \infty\}$.

steps.slogan: Let $t \to \infty$ in $\mathbb{E} M_{t \wedge \tau} = 1$ with dominated convergence.
steps.detail: On $\{\tau < \infty\}$ the stopped martingale tends to $M_\tau = e^{\theta x}$ because $X_\tau = 0$. On $\{\tau = \infty\}$ it tends to $0$. The constant bound $e^{\theta x}$ gives $1 = e^{\theta x} P(\tau < \infty)$, which is the [ruin probability](c:ruin-probability) formula.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: The surplus is a Brownian motion with drift, and its Gaussian increments drive the martingale.
concepts.c:ruin-probability: The theorem computes the probability that the surplus ever reaches 0.
concepts.c:martingale: The exponential martingale has constant mean 1, which fixes the ruin probability.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The ruin time is a stopping time, so optional stopping applies at $t \wedge \tau$.
concepts.c:almost-sure-convergence: The almost sure limit $B_t/t \to 0$ shows that the martingale vanishes without ruin.

source.ref: P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion (Cambridge University Press 2010, authors' version), Exercise 2.16, p. 62, and its solution in Hints and solutions for selected exercises, p. 368.
source.note: The solution uses the martingale exp(2bB(t) − 2b²t) and the boundedness of the stopped process. These steps follow it with a = x/σ and b = µ/σ, and they add the law of large numbers that makes the martingale vanish without ruin.

new_concepts.name: compound Poisson process
new_concepts.reminder: A compound Poisson process adds up iid random jumps at the arrival times of a Poisson process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(N_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) with rate $\lambda>0$, and let $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ be [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) that are independent of $(N_t)$. The compound Poisson process is $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N_t}Y_i$, with $S_t=0$ when $N_t=0$. It has independent and stationary increments, and $E[e^{i\theta S_t}]=\exp(\lambda t(\varphi_Y(\theta)-1))$, where $\varphi_Y$ is the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of $Y_1$.

new_concepts.name: Cramer-Lundberg model
new_concepts.reminder: The Cramér–Lundberg model describes the capital of an insurer as initial capital plus premiums minus compound Poisson claims.
new_concepts.definition: In the Cramér–Lundberg model, claims arrive at the times of a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) $(N_t)$ with rate $\lambda>0$, the claim sizes $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are positive [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) with mean $\mu$ and independent of $(N_t)$, and premiums come in at a constant rate $c>0$. The risk process with initial capital $u\ge0$ is $R_t=u+ct-S_t$, where $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N_t}X_i$ is a [compound Poisson process](c:compound-poisson-process). The net profit condition $c>\lambda\mu$ means that $R_t\to\infty$ almost surely.

new_concepts.name: ruin probability
new_concepts.reminder: The ruin probability $\psi(u)$ is the probability that the capital of an insurer, started at $u$, ever falls below zero.
new_concepts.definition: For a risk process $R_t=u+ct-S_t$, as in the [Cramér–Lundberg model](c:cramer-lundberg-model), the ruin time is the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:R_t<0\}$, and the (infinite-horizon) ruin probability is $\psi(u)=P(\tau(u)<\infty)$ for initial capital $u\ge0$. The finite-horizon ruin probability is $\psi(u,T)=P(\tau(u)\le T)$. Equivalently, $\psi(u)=P(\sup_{t\ge0}(S_t-ct)>u)$.

statement: In the [Cramér–Lundberg model](c:cramer-lundberg-model) with net profit, the first [ladder height](c:ladder-height) of the claim surplus has the defective density $(\lambda/c)\,\bar B(y)$, so the [ruin probability](c:ruin-probability) from zero reserve is $\rho = \lambda\mu_B/c$.

hypotheses.text: Claims arrive at the jump times of a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) of rate $\lambda$, independent of the claim sizes.
The claim sizes are [independent](c:independent-random-variables), identically distributed and nonnegative, with tail $\bar B$ and finite mean $\mu_B$.
The premium rate $c$ is above the [expected](c:expected-value) claim amount per unit time: $\rho = \lambda\mu_B/c < 1$.

conclusion: $P(\tau_+ < \infty,\ S(\tau_+) > z) = \frac{\lambda}{c}\int_z^\infty \bar B(y)\,dy$ for every $z \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Time reversal and Poisson ladder points
proofs.slogan: Reverse the walk so that its ladder points form a Poisson process, then decompose at the first step below zero.
proofs.scope: The full statement.

roles.why: Exponential times between claims give the steps of the reversed walk an exponential right tail, so its ladder heights are exponential.
Independent claims make the claim surplus at claim times a [random walk](c:random-walk), and the claim tail enters the final integral.
A positive mean step of the reversed walk makes it reach a new maximum with probability one.

steps.slogan: Look at the claim surplus only just after each claim.
steps.detail: The claim surplus decreases between claims, so it first exceeds 0 at a claim time. The values $S_n$ just after claims form a [random walk](c:random-walk) with steps $Y_i - cE_i$, and $\bar S_n = -S_n$ has positive mean step $1/\alpha - \mu_B$ with $\alpha = \lambda/c$.

steps.slogan: Show that the steps of the reflected walk have an exponential right tail.
steps.detail: Because $cE$ is exponential with rate $\alpha$ and independent of $Y$, $P(cE - Y > x) = a e^{-\alpha x}$ for $x \ge 0$, with $a = P(cE - Y > 0)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the ladder heights of the reflected walk form a Poisson process of rate $\alpha$.
steps.detail: The strong law makes the first ladder epoch of $\bar S$ finite, and the exponential tail makes each ladder height an [exponential](c:exponential-distribution) variable of rate $\alpha$. So the expected number of ladder points in $[0, w]$ is $1 + \alpha w$.

steps.slogan: Reverse time and decompose at the first step that falls to or below zero.
steps.detail: Time reversal turns the probability that $\bar S$ stays positive up to time $n$ into the probability that $n$ is a ladder epoch. Summing over $n$ gives $P(\tau < \infty, \bar S_\tau \le x) = F(x) + \alpha\int_{-\infty}^x F(y)\,dy$ for $x \le 0$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the step tail to get the integrated claim tail.
steps.detail: With $g(u) = P(Y - cE \ge u)$, Tonelli gives $g(z) + \alpha\int_z^\infty g(u)\,du = \alpha\int_z^\infty \bar B(y)\,dy$. The value at $z = 0$ is $\alpha\mu_B = \rho$.

concepts.c:cramer-lundberg-model: The theorem is about the claim surplus of the Cramér–Lundberg risk model.
concepts.c:ladder-height: The result gives the law of the first ladder height of the claim surplus.
concepts.c:ruin-probability: The total mass of the ladder height law is the ruin probability from zero reserve.
concepts.c:poisson-process: Poisson claim arrivals make the ladder points of the reflected walk a Poisson process.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independent claims and interarrival times make the embedded surplus a random walk.
concepts.c:expected-value: The net profit condition compares the expected claims per unit time with the premium rate.
concepts.c:random-walk: The proof works with the claim surplus just after claims, which is a random walk.
concepts.c:exponential-distribution: The memoryless exponential tail makes each ladder height of the reflected walk exponential.

source.ref: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition, Example 5.8.15 and Lemma 5.8.13, pp. 327-329, formula (5.8.2) on p. 329.
source.note: The steps follow the source derivation of formula (5.8.2) for the M/G/1 walk. The final integration that turns (5.8.2) into the integrated claim tail is added.

new_concepts.name: exponential distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ on $[0,\infty)$ and no memory.
new_concepts.definition: For $\lambda>0$, the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ is the law on $[0,\infty)$ with [probability density function](c:probability-density-function) $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, so $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ and $E[X]=1/\lambda$. Among laws of positive random variables, it is the only one with the memoryless property $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$ for all $s,t\ge0$.

new_concepts.name: ladder height
new_concepts.reminder: A ladder height is the value of a random walk at the first time it exceeds its previous maximum.
new_concepts.definition: Let $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$ be a [random walk](c:random-walk) with $S_0=0$. The first strict ascending ladder epoch is the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau_+=\inf\{n\ge1:S_n>0\}$, and the first ladder height is $H=S_{\tau_+}$ on the event $\{\tau_+<\infty\}$. The later ladder heights $H_k=S_{\tau_k}$ at the successive strict ascending ladder epochs $\tau_k$ are the record values of $(S_n)$, and the increments $H_k-H_{k-1}$ are iid with the law of $H$ while new records occur.

statement: In a [queue](c:queueing-system) with [independent](c:independent-random-variables) increments $U_n$, the waiting times of Lindley's recursion $W_n = \max(W_{n-1} + U_n, 0)$, $W_0 = 0$, equal the maximum of a reversed [random walk](c:random-walk), have the law of $M_n = \max_{k \le n} S_k$, and increase in law to $M = \sup_k S_k$.

hypotheses.text: The increments $U_1, U_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and identically distributed real random variables.
For the last claim, $\mathbb{E}|U_1| < \infty$ and the [expected value](c:expected-value) $\mathbb{E}U_1$ is negative.

conclusion: $W_n = S_n - \min_{i \le n} S_i$, $W_n$ has the law of $M_n$, and $P(W_n > x) \uparrow P(M > x)$. If $\mathbb{E}U_1 < 0$, then $M < \infty$ almost surely and $W_n \to M$ in [distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution).

proofs.name: Unfolding the recursion and reversing time
proofs.slogan: Unfold the recursion into a maximum of partial sums that end at time $n$, then reverse the increments, which does not change their joint law.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The first three claims hold for every increment law. The finiteness of $M$ needs an integrable increment with negative mean.

roles.why: Independent and identically distributed increments have a product law that does not change when the order is reversed.
A negative mean makes the [random walk](c:random-walk) drift to $-\infty$, so its supremum is finite.

steps.slogan: Unfold Lindley's recursion into a maximum of partial sums that end at time $n$.
steps.detail: By induction, if $W_{n-1} = \max_{0 \le k \le n-1}(U_{n-k} + \dots + U_{n-1})$, then adding $U_n$ and taking the maximum with 0 gives $W_n = \max_{0 \le k \le n}(U_{n-k+1} + \dots + U_n) = S_n - \min_{i \le n} S_i$.

steps.slogan: Reverse the order of the increments, which keeps their joint law.
steps.detail: The vector $(U_n, \dots, U_1)$ has the same [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) as $(U_1, \dots, U_n)$ because the product law is symmetric. The same function of the two vectors gives $W_n$ and $M_n$, so they have the same law.

steps.slogan: Let $n \to \infty$ in the nondecreasing running maximum $M_n$.
steps.detail: The running maximum increases pathwise to $M$, so the events $\{M_n > x\}$ increase to $\{M > x\}$, and continuity of the measure gives $P(W_n > x) \uparrow P(M > x)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the supremum $M$ is finite when the mean increment is negative.
steps.detail: The strong law gives $S_k/k \to \mathbb{E}U_1 < 0$, so $S_k \to -\infty$ and only finitely many $S_k$ are positive. Hence $M < \infty$ almost surely, and $P(W_n \le x) \to P(M \le x)$ for every $x$ is [convergence in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to a proper law.

concepts.c:queueing-system: Lindley's recursion is the waiting time equation of the single-server queue.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independent increments make the reversed increment vector equal in law to the original one.
concepts.c:random-walk: The waiting time is the running maximum of the random walk of the increments.
concepts.c:expected-value: The sign of the mean increment decides whether the supremum is finite.
concepts.c:probability-distribution: Reversal preserves the joint distribution of the increments, which gives the equality in law.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: The waiting times converge in distribution to the supremum of the walk.

source.ref: R. G. Gallager, Discrete Stochastic Processes, MIT OpenCourseWare 6.262 notes (Spring 2011), Chapter 7, equations (7.4) to (7.8) and Theorem 7.2.1, pp. 318-319.
source.note: The source iterates the recursion, reverses the increments and uses monotonicity in n. These steps add the strong law argument for a finite supremum.

new_concepts.name: queueing system
new_concepts.reminder: A queueing system models customers who arrive, wait in line and get service from one or more servers.
new_concepts.definition: A queueing system is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) model given by an arrival process of customers, a law of service times, a number $s$ of servers, a capacity of the waiting room and a service discipline, such as first come, first served. Kendall's notation $A/B/s$ names the interarrival law $A$, the service law $B$ and $s$, with $M$ for exponential (memoryless) laws and $G$ for general laws. Its main processes are the number $Q(t)$ of customers in the system and the waiting times $W_n$ of the customers.

statement: For a [random walk](c:random-walk) with i.i.d. steps, the [generating function](c:generating-function) of the laws of the maxima $M_n$ equals the exponential of a series in the laws of $S_n^+$, both in the measure [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) and for [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function).

hypotheses.text: The steps $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and identically distributed real random variables with law $f$.
The variable $x$ is complex with $|x| < 1$, so the [power series](c:power-series) in $x$ converge in norm.

conclusion: $\sum_{n \ge 0} x^n E[e^{i\theta M_n}] = \exp\Big(\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{x^n}{n} E[e^{i\theta S_n^+}]\Big)$ for real $\theta$, and the same identity holds for the laws in the measure algebra.

proofs.name: Projection in the measure algebra
proofs.slogan: Write the Lindley recursion as an equation in the measure algebra and split it with the projection onto measures on $[0, \infty)$.
proofs.scope: The full statement, for every step law and every $|x| < 1$.

roles.why: Independent steps make the law of the next reflected position a [convolution](c:convolution) with $f$, and make reversal of the steps keep the law.
With $|x| < 1$ the series $G$ and $L$ and the exponential series converge in total variation norm.

steps.slogan: Split the measure algebra with the projection that moves negative mass to zero.
steps.detail: The image $P\mu$ under $y \mapsto \max(y, 0)$ is a norm-one projection. Its range (measures on $[0,\infty)$) and its kernel (measures on $(-\infty, 0]$ with mass $0$) are closed subalgebras with intersection $\{0\}$.

steps.slogan: Write the law of the maximum through the Lindley recursion $g_{n+1} = P(g_n * f)$.
steps.detail: The reflected walk $W_{n+1} = \max(W_n + X_{n+1}, 0)$ has law $g_{n+1} = P(g_n * f)$, and reversal of the steps shows that $W_n$ has the law of $M_n$.

steps.slogan: Sum the recursion into one equation for the generating series $G$.
steps.detail: With $G = \sum_n x^n g_n$ and $A = \delta_0 - x f$, the recursion gives $P(G * A) = \delta_0$, so $G * A = \delta_0 + m$ with $m$ in the kernel of $P$.

steps.slogan: Factor $A$ as a product of exponentials of the two projected parts of $L$.
steps.detail: The logarithm series gives $A = \exp(-L)$ with $L = \sum_n x^n f^{*n}/n$. Commutativity splits it as $\exp(-PL) * \exp(-(I-P)L)$, so $G * \exp(-PL) = (\delta_0 + m) * \exp((I-P)L)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two sides of the factored equation in the two subalgebras.
steps.detail: The left side lies in the range of $P$ and the right side in $\delta_0$ plus the kernel of $P$. Their difference from $\delta_0$ is in both subalgebras, so it is $0$ and $G = \exp(PL)$.

steps.slogan: Take [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function) of the measure identity.
steps.detail: The map $\mu \mapsto \int e^{i\theta y}\,\mu(dy)$ is a bounded unital homomorphism of the measure algebra, so it maps the identity $G = \exp(PL)$ term by term to the classical form.

concepts.c:random-walk: The identity describes the running maximum of a random walk with i.i.d. steps.
concepts.c:generating-function: Both sides are generating functions in $x$ of sequences of laws or of transforms.
concepts.c:banach-algebra: The proof works in the Banach algebra of finite measures under convolution.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: Characteristic functions turn the measure identity into the classical scalar form.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence of the steps makes the Lindley recursion a convolution recursion.
concepts.c:power-series: Power series in $x$ with $|x| < 1$ define $G$, $L$ and the exponential in norm.
concepts.c:convolution: The law of a sum of independent variables is the convolution of their laws.

source.note: The steps write out, for the projection y ↦ max(y, 0) on ℝ, the Banach algebra argument behind Lemma 1 of J. F. C. Kingman, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 2 (1962), pp. 345-346, which restates results of J. G. Wendel. The source quotes the lemma without proof.

statement: For a [renewal process](c:renewal-process) with [independent](c:independent-random-variables) identically distributed cycle pairs $(r_i, t_i)$, the reward per unit time $R(t)/t$ converges [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence) to $E r_1 / E t_1$.

hypotheses.text: The pairs $(r_i, t_i)$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and identically distributed. The reward $r_i$ can depend on the cycle length $t_i$.
The cycle lengths satisfy $t_i \ge 0$ and $0 < E t_1 < \infty$, and the rewards satisfy $E|r_1| < \infty$, so both have a finite [expected value](c:expected-value).

conclusion: $R(t)/t = \frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{N(t)} r_i \to E r_1 / E t_1$ almost surely as $t \to \infty$.

proofs.name: Multiply and divide by the number of cycles
proofs.slogan: Write $R(t)/t$ as the mean reward per cycle times the number of cycles per unit time, and apply the strong law to each factor.
proofs.scope: The full statement.

roles.why: Independence of the cycles lets the strong law of large numbers act on the lengths and on the rewards.
Finite means are what the strong law needs, and a positive mean length makes the number of cycles finite at each time.

steps.slogan: Show that the number of completed cycles is finite and grows without bound.
steps.detail: The strong law gives $T_n/n \to E t_1 > 0$ almost surely, so $T_n \to \infty$ and $N(t)$ is finite. Since each $T_n$ is finite, $N(t)$ is nondecreasing and $N(t) \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze $t$ between two renewal times to get the cycle rate.
steps.detail: From $T_{N(t)} \le t < T_{N(t)+1}$, the ratios $T_{N(t)}/N(t)$ and $T_{N(t)+1}/N(t)$ bound $t/N(t)$, and both tend to $E t_1$. So $N(t)/t \to 1/E t_1$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Apply the strong law to the rewards along the random index $N(t)$.
steps.detail: The averages $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \le n} r_i$ tend to $E r_1$, and $N(t) \to \infty$ through the integers, so $R(t)/N(t) \to E r_1$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Multiply the two limits on an event of probability one.
steps.detail: On the intersection of the three events of probability one, $R(t)/t = (R(t)/N(t)) \cdot (N(t)/t)$ for large $t$, and the product of the limits is $E r_1 / E t_1$.

concepts.c:renewal-process: The cycle ends form a renewal process whose counting function $N(t)$ sets the number of rewards.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence of the cycle pairs is what the strong law of large numbers needs.
concepts.c:almost-sure-convergence: Each limit in the proof holds on an event of probability one, and so does their product.
concepts.c:expected-value: The limit is the ratio of the expected reward per cycle to the expected cycle length.

source.ref: Rick Durrett, Essentials of Stochastic Processes, 2nd edition, Theorem 3.1 (p. 102) and Theorem 3.3 (p. 103) with their proofs.
source.note: The steps follow the source proofs of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3. The finiteness of N(t) and the passage of the strong law along N(t) are written out.

new_concepts.name: renewal process
new_concepts.reminder: A renewal process counts the events of a sequence whose gaps are independent and identically distributed positive times.
new_concepts.definition: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be positive [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables), and let $S_0=0$ and $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$. The renewal process is the [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $N(t)=\#\{n\ge1:S_n\le t\}$, $t\ge0$, which counts the renewal times $S_n$ in $[0,t]$. The $X_i$ are the interarrival times, and their common law $F$ is the interarrival distribution.

statement: For an integer-valued [renewal process](c:renewal-process) whose step law has support with [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) 1 and mean $\mu \in [1, \infty]$, the probability $u_n$ that $n$ is a renewal tends to $1/\mu$.

hypotheses.text: The step law satisfies $f_k \ge 0$ for $k \ge 1$ and $\sum_k f_k = 1$, with [mean](c:expected-value) $\mu = \sum_k k f_k \in [1, \infty]$.
The [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) of $\{k : f_k > 0\}$ is 1.
The sequence $u$ solves $u_0 = 1$ and $u_n = \sum_{k=1}^n f_k u_{n-k}$ for $n \ge 1$, so $\sum_{k \le n} u_k$ is the [renewal function](c:renewal-function) at $n$.

conclusion: $u_n \to 1/\mu$ as $n \to \infty$, with $1/\infty = 0$.

proofs.name: Elementary proof of Erdős, Feller and Pollard
proofs.slogan: Along a sequence where $u_n$ tends to its limit superior, shifts by support points keep the limit, and the tail identity turns this into $\lambda\mu \le 1$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for finite and infinite mean. The lower bound step is needed only when $\mu < \infty$.

roles.why: The tail sums of the step law add up to the mean, and the tail identity has these sums as weights.
A [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) of 1 makes every large integer a sum of support points, so all large shifts keep the limit.
The renewal equation drives the shift argument and sums to the tail identity.

steps.slogan: Bound $u_n$ by 1 and sum the renewal equation into a tail identity.
steps.detail: By induction $0 \le u_n \le 1$. With $r_k = \sum_{j > k} f_j$, the differences of $D_n = \sum_{k=0}^n r_k u_{n-k}$ vanish by the renewal equation, so $\sum_{k=0}^n r_k u_{n-k} = 1$ for all $n$, and $\sum_k r_k = \mu$.

steps.slogan: Show that shifts by support points keep the [limit superior](c:limit-superior) along a maximizing sequence.
steps.detail: Let $u_{n_v} \to \lambda = \limsup u_n$ and $f_j > 0$. If $u_{n_v - j}$ had a smaller limit point $\lambda'$, the renewal equation would give $\lambda \le (1 - f_j)\lambda + f_j \lambda'$, a contradiction. So $u_{n_v - j} \to \lambda$, and by induction $u_{n_v - s} \to \lambda$ for every finite sum $s$ of support points.

steps.slogan: Write every large integer as a sum of support points with Bézout's identity.
steps.detail: Finitely many support points $a_1, \dots, a_t$ have greatest common divisor 1, so $\sum_i c_i a_i = 1$ for some integers $c_i$. Every $n \ge N_0 = (a_1 - 1)\sum_i |c_i| a_i$ is then a nonnegative integer combination of the $a_i$.

steps.slogan: Combine the shifts with the tail identity to get $\lambda\mu \le 1$.
steps.detail: At index $n_v - N_0$ the tail identity gives $1 \ge \sum_{k \le M} r_k u_{n_v - N_0 - k}$, and each term tends to $r_k\lambda$. So $\lambda\sum_{k \le M} r_k \le 1$ for every $M$, and $\lambda\mu \le 1$. If $\mu = \infty$, this gives $u_n \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the shift argument with the [limit inferior](c:limit-inferior) when the mean is finite.
steps.detail: With the lower bound $\max(\lambda_* - \varepsilon, 0)$, the shift argument gives $u_{n'_v - s} \to \lambda_* = \liminf u_n$ for $s \ge N_0$. Since $u_n \le 1$, the tail identity gives $1 \le \lambda_* \sum_{k \le M} r_k + \sum_{k > M} r_k$, so $\lambda_*\mu \ge 1$. Together with the upper bound, $u_n \to 1/\mu$.

concepts.c:renewal-process: The renewals are the partial sums of the integer steps, and $u_n$ is the chance that $n$ is one of them.
concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: The gcd condition excludes periodic step laws, for which $u_n$ has no limit.
concepts.c:expected-value: The mean step $\mu$ fixes the limit density $1/\mu$ of renewals.
concepts.c:renewal-function: The partial sums of $u_n$ form the renewal function, and $u_n$ is its increment.
concepts.c:limit-superior: The proof first identifies the limit superior of $u_n$ along a maximizing sequence.
concepts.c:limit-inferior: For finite mean the same argument applied to the limit inferior gives the lower bound.

new_concepts.name: renewal function
new_concepts.reminder: The renewal function gives the expected number of renewals up to time $t$.
new_concepts.definition: For a [renewal process](c:renewal-process) with interarrival distribution $F$ and renewal times $S_n$, the renewal function is $U(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}F^{*n}(t)=E[\#\{n\ge0:S_n\le t\}]$ for $t\ge0$, where $F^{*n}$ is the $n$-fold [convolution](c:convolution) power and $F^{*0}$ is the point mass at $0$. It counts the renewal at time $0$, so $U(t)=1+E[N(t)]$, and some authors call $m(t)=E[N(t)]=U(t)-1$ the renewal function.

new_concepts.name: renewal process
new_concepts.reminder: A renewal process counts the events of a sequence whose gaps are independent and identically distributed positive times.
new_concepts.definition: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be positive [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables), and let $S_0=0$ and $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$. The renewal process is the [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $N(t)=\#\{n\ge1:S_n\le t\}$, $t\ge0$, which counts the renewal times $S_n$ in $[0,t]$. The $X_i$ are the interarrival times, and their common law $F$ is the interarrival distribution.

statement: For a [random walk](c:random-walk) $S_n$ with independent steps that are not almost surely zero, the exit index $J$ from $(\beta, \alpha)$ is finite almost surely, and $\mathbb{E}[e^{rS_J - J\gamma(r)}] = 1$ for every $r$ where the [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) $e^{\gamma(r)}$ is finite.

hypotheses.text: The steps $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and identically distributed, and $P(X_1 \ne 0) > 0$.
The thresholds satisfy $\beta < 0 < \alpha$, and $J = \min\{n \ge 1 : S_n \ge \alpha \text{ or } S_n \le \beta\}$.
The real number $r$ satisfies $\mathbb{E} e^{rX_1} < \infty$, and $\gamma(r) = \ln \mathbb{E} e^{rX_1}$.

conclusion: $J < \infty$ almost surely with geometric tails, and $\mathbb{E}[\exp(rS_J - J\gamma(r))] = 1$.

proofs.name: Exponential tilting of the step law
proofs.slogan: Under the tilted step law the exit index is still finite, and its law equals the original expectation of $e^{rS_n - n\gamma(r)}$ on $\{J = n\}$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every step law that is not the point mass at 0, and every $r$ with a finite moment generating function.

roles.why: Independence makes disjoint blocks of steps independent, and it makes the tilted product law have the density $e^{rs_n - n\gamma(r)}$.
Two finite thresholds let one block of large steps force an exit from $(\beta, \alpha)$.
A finite [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) at $r$ makes the tilted law a probability measure.

steps.slogan: Show that the exit index $J$ has geometric tails by a block argument.
steps.detail: Pick $\delta > 0$ with $p = P(X_1 > \delta) > 0$, or the mirror case, and $m\delta \ge \alpha - \beta$. A block of $m$ steps above $\delta$ forces an exit, and the blocks are independent, so $P(J > km) \le (1 - p^m)^k$.

steps.slogan: Define the tilted step law $F_r(dx) = e^{rx - \gamma(r)} F(dx)$.
steps.detail: Because $\mathbb{E} e^{rX_1} = e^{\gamma(r)}$ is finite, $F_r$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure). Its density is strictly positive, so $F_r$ and $F$ have the same null sets, and $F_r$ is not the point mass at 0.

steps.slogan: Write the tilted probability of $\{J = n\}$ as an original expectation.
steps.detail: The exit index is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time), so $\{J = n\}$ is a Borel set $A_n$ of $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$. By Tonelli's theorem the tilted product law has density $e^{rs_n - n\gamma(r)}$, so $P_r(J = n) = \mathbb{E}[e^{rS_n - n\gamma(r)}; J = n]$.

steps.slogan: Sum over $n$ and use that $J$ is finite under both laws.
steps.detail: The block argument applies to the tilted walk, so $\sum_n P_r(J = n) = 1$. It also gives $J < \infty$ under the original law, and monotone convergence turns the sum of the right sides into $\mathbb{E}[e^{rS_J - J\gamma(r)}]$.

concepts.c:random-walk: The identity concerns the random walk of partial sums at its exit index.
concepts.c:moment-generating-function: The logarithm of the moment generating function is the compensator $\gamma(r)$ in the identity.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independent steps give independent blocks and a product density for the tilted law.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The tilted step law is a probability measure with the same null sets as the original law.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The exit index is a stopping time, so each event $\{J = n\}$ depends on the first $n$ steps only.

source.note: The source proves the identity for discrete steps with the tilted PMF and remarks that the general case replaces sums by Stieltjes integrals. These steps treat a general step law with product measures.

statement: For a $d$-dimensional process $X$ whose components are continuous [semimartingales](c:semimartingale) and $F \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, almost surely for all $t \ge 0$, $F(X_t) = F(X_0) + \sum_i \int_0^t \partial_i F(X_s)\,dX^i_s + \frac12\sum_{i,j}\int_0^t \partial_i\partial_j F(X_s)\,d\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_s$, with [stochastic integrals](c:stochastic-integral) and [quadratic covariations](c:quadratic-variation).

hypotheses.text: Each component $X^i = M^i + A^i$ is a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale): a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) plus a continuous adapted process of [finite variation](c:bounded-variation).
$F\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is twice continuously differentiable.

conclusion: Almost surely, for all $t \ge 0$, $F(X_t) - F(X_0) = \sum_i \int_0^t \partial_i F(X_s)\,dX^i_s + \frac12\sum_{i,j}\int_0^t \partial_i\partial_j F(X_s)\,d\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_s$.

proofs.name: Second-order Taylor expansion along partitions
proofs.slogan: Expand $F$ to second order along a fine partition, then identify the first-order sum as a stochastic integral and the second-order sum as a bracket integral.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for all times simultaneously.

roles.why: The local martingale part gives the stochastic integral and the bracket, and the finite-variation part gives an ordinary integral.
Continuity of the second derivatives gives the Taylor remainder and makes the remainder error small uniformly.

steps.slogan: Telescope $F(X_t) - F(X_0)$ over a partition and expand each increment to second order.
steps.detail: Taylor's theorem with integral remainder writes each increment as $\nabla F(X_{t_k})\cdot\Delta X_k + \Delta X_k^{T} R_k \Delta X_k$, where $R_k$ averages $\nabla^2 F$ over the segment between $X_{t_k}$ and $X_{t_{k+1}}$. This splits the total change into a first-order sum and a second-order sum.

steps.slogan: Show that left-point Riemann sums converge to the [stochastic integral](c:stochastic-integral).
steps.detail: After stopping, the step integrand differs from the continuous integrand by a bounded amount that tends to 0 uniformly. The isometry and dominated convergence control the martingale part, and the total variation controls the other part. So the first-order sum converges in [probability](c:convergence-in-probability).

steps.slogan: Replace the averaged Hessian by its value at the left endpoint with a vanishing error.
steps.detail: Uniform continuity of $\nabla^2 F$ on a compact set that contains the path makes the largest Hessian error tend to 0 almost surely. The sum of squared increments stays bounded in probability, so Slutsky's theorem kills the product.

steps.slogan: Identify the frozen second-order sum with an integral against the [quadratic covariation](c:quadratic-variation).
steps.detail: Polarization writes the measures of products of increments as differences of measures of squared increments. Along a subsequence their distribution functions converge almost surely on a dense set of times, and Helly-Bray gives convergence of the integrals of the continuous function $\partial_i\partial_j F(X)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the limits in probability and extend from fixed times to all times by continuity.
steps.detail: The exact identity holds for every partition, and the right side converges in probability to the Itô expression. So the formula holds almost surely at each rational time, and continuity of both sides in $t$ gives it for all times at once.

concepts.c:semimartingale: The formula holds for continuous semimartingales and shows that $F(X)$ is again one.
concepts.c:stochastic-integral: The first-order term of the formula is a stochastic integral.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The second-order correction integrates against the quadratic covariation of the components.
concepts.c:local-martingale: The local martingale part of $X$ produces the bracket and the stochastic integral.
concepts.c:bounded-variation: The finite-variation part of $X$ contributes an ordinary Stieltjes integral and no bracket.
concepts.c:convergence-in-probability: Riemann sums and quadratic sums converge to their limits in probability.

source.note: The notes use a mean-value point for the remainder. These steps use the integral form of the remainder and prove the Riemann sum convergence from the isometry.

new_concepts.name: local martingale
new_concepts.reminder: A local martingale becomes a martingale when you stop it at suitable stopping times that increase to infinity.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a local martingale when there are [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau_1\le\tau_2\le\dots$ with $\tau_n\to\infty$ almost surely such that each stopped process $(M_{t\wedge\tau_n}-M_0)_{t\ge0}$ is a [martingale](c:martingale). Such a sequence $(\tau_n)$ is a localizing sequence. A local martingale that is not a martingale is a strict local martingale.

new_concepts.name: quadratic variation
new_concepts.reminder: The quadratic variation of a process is the limit of its sums of squared increments over finer partitions.
new_concepts.definition: For a [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$ and partitions $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_k=t$ of $[0,t]$ with mesh tending to $0$, the quadratic variation is $[X]_t=\lim\sum_i(X_{t_{i+1}}-X_{t_i})^2$, where the limit exists in probability. For a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) $M$, $[M]=\langle M\rangle$ is the unique continuous increasing adapted process with $\langle M\rangle_0=0$ such that $M^2-\langle M\rangle$ is a local martingale. A continuous path of finite variation has quadratic variation $0$.

new_concepts.name: semimartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A semimartingale is a local martingale plus an adapted process of finite variation.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $X$ is a semimartingale when $X_t=X_0+M_t+A_t$, where $M$ is a [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $M_0=0$ and $A$ is an adapted càdlàg process with $A_0=0$ whose paths have [bounded variation](c:bounded-variation) on every bounded interval. The decomposition is not unique in general, but a continuous $X$ has exactly one decomposition with continuous $M$ and $A$. By the Bichteler–Dellacherie theorem, the semimartingales are exactly the good integrators for stochastic integrals.

statement: A continuous adapted process $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) for its [filtration](c:filtration) if and only if each component is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) and the [quadratic covariations](c:quadratic-variation) are $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij} t$.

hypotheses.text: $X = (X^1, \dots, X^d)$ is continuous and adapted to the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_t)$.
For the converse direction, each $X^i$ is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij} t$.

conclusion: $X$ is a $d$-dimensional $(\mathcal{F}_t)$-Brownian motion exactly when its components are continuous local martingales with $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij} t$.

proofs.name: Complex exponential martingale
proofs.slogan: Itô's formula makes $\exp(i\xi\cdot X_t + |\xi|^2 t/2)$ a bounded martingale, which fixes the conditional characteristic function of each increment.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The direct direction is a computation of conditional moments.

roles.why: Adaptedness and continuity are part of the definition of an $(\mathcal{F}_t)$-Brownian motion and are needed for Itô's formula.
The brackets $\delta_{ij} t$ make the drift of the exponential cancel exactly.

steps.slogan: Compute conditional moments of Brownian increments to get the martingale and bracket properties.
steps.detail: With $Y = X - X_0$, [independent increments](c:independent-increments) with mean 0 and covariance $(t-s)I$ make $Y^i$ and $Y^iY^j - \delta_{ij}t$ martingales. Uniqueness of the bracket gives $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij}t$.

steps.slogan: Show with Itô's formula that the complex exponential of $X$ is a local martingale.
steps.detail: For $Z_t = \exp(i\xi\cdot X_t + |\xi|^2 t/2)$, the time derivative term $\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}Z\,dt$ cancels the bracket term $-\frac12\sum_{j,k}\xi_j\xi_k Z\,d\langle X^j, X^k\rangle$. Only the stochastic integral remains.

steps.slogan: Upgrade the bounded local martingale on $[0,T]$ to a true martingale.
steps.detail: On $[0,T]$ the modulus of $Z$ is at most $e^{|\xi|^2T/2}$. Dominated convergence along a localizing sequence gives $\mathbb{E}[Z_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s] = Z_s$, so $\mathbb{E}[e^{i\xi\cdot(X_t - X_s)}\mid\mathcal{F}_s] = e^{-|\xi|^2(t-s)/2}$.

steps.slogan: Read off independence and the [normal law](c:normal-distribution) from the joint [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function).
steps.detail: For any $\mathcal{F}_s$-measurable vector $W$, the joint characteristic function of $W$ and $X_t - X_s$ factors into that of $W$ times the Gaussian one. Uniqueness of characteristic functions gives independence from $\mathcal{F}_s$ and the law $N(0,(t-s)I)$.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: The theorem characterizes Brownian motion among continuous processes.
concepts.c:filtration: Brownian motion is defined relative to the filtration that the local martingales use.
concepts.c:local-martingale: The components are only assumed to be continuous local martingales.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The brackets $\delta_{ij}t$ carry all the information that the theorem needs.
concepts.c:independent-increments: Independence of increments from the past is the conclusion of the converse direction.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: Each increment has the centered normal law with covariance $(t-s)I$.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: The conditional characteristic function of an increment identifies its law and its independence.

statement: For $p > 0$ there are constants $0 < c_p \le C_p$ such that every continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) $M$ with $M_0 = 0$ and every [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $T$ satisfy $c_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2} \le \mathbb{E}(M^*_T)^p \le C_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2}$, where $\langle M\rangle$ is the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation).

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $M_0 = 0$.
$T$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time), possibly infinite, and $p > 0$.

conclusion: $c_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2} \le \mathbb{E}\sup_{t \le T}|M_t|^p \le C_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2}$ with $C_p = 2^{p(p+1)/2+p+1}$ and $c_p = 2^{-p^2/4-2p-1}$.

proofs.name: Exit estimate and good-lambda inequalities
proofs.slogan: Bound the chance that one of $M^2$ and $\langle M\rangle$ is large while the other is small, then integrate the tails.
proofs.scope: Both inequalities for every $p > 0$ and every stopping time.

roles.why: Both $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ and $\langle M\rangle - M^2$ are continuous local martingales, which feeds the exit estimate.
The stopped process $M^T$ is again a continuous local martingale, so the bound at $T = \infty$ gives the general case.

steps.slogan: Bound the probability that a local martingale exits up before it exits down.
steps.detail: The [martingale](c:martingale) stopped at the exit of $(-b, a)$ is bounded and has mean 0, and its limit is $a$ on an up-exit and at least $-b$ otherwise. This gives $P(T_a < T_{-b}) \le \frac{b}{a+b}P(N^*_\infty > 0)$.

steps.slogan: Compare two nonnegative processes whose difference is a local martingale.
steps.detail: If $X$ reaches $\alpha$ while $Y$ stays below $\beta$, then $X - Y$ reaches $\alpha - \beta$ without reaching $-\beta$. The exit estimate bounds this event by $(\beta/\alpha)P((X-Y)^*_\infty > 0)$.

steps.slogan: Derive the two good-lambda inequalities by restarting $M$ at a threshold time.
steps.detail: Restarting $M$ when $|M|$ reaches $\sqrt r$ gives $P((M^*)^2 \ge 4r, \langle M\rangle < br) \le bP((M^*)^2 \ge r)$. Restarting when the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) reaches $r$ gives $P(\langle M\rangle \ge 2r, (M^*)^2 < br) \le 4bP(\langle M\rangle \ge r)$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the good-lambda bounds against $r^{p/2-1}\,dr$ and absorb the small term.
steps.detail: The tail formula $\mathbb{E}X^q = \kappa^q\int_0^\infty qr^{q-1}P(X \ge \kappa r)\,dr$ turns each tail bound into a moment bound. A small $b$ moves the term $b\,\mathbb{E}(M^*)^p$ or $4b\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle^{p/2}$ to the left side when it is finite.

steps.slogan: Remove the finiteness assumptions by stopping and pass to a general stopping time.
steps.detail: Stopping when $|M|$ or $\langle M\rangle$ reaches $n$ makes the needed moment finite. Monotone convergence as $n \to \infty$ gives both bounds, and applying them to $M^T$ gives them at the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $T$.

concepts.c:local-martingale: The inequality holds for every continuous local martingale started at 0.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The inequality holds at every stopping time, which also makes localization possible.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The quadratic variation is the quantity whose moments are compared with those of the maximum.
concepts.c:martingale: The exit estimate uses the mean-zero property of a bounded stopped martingale.

steps.slogan: Record that nonnegative local martingales such as $\mathcal{E}(M)$ are supermartingales with mean at most 1.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ is bounded above and converges, with $\mathbb{E}e^{M_\infty/2} \le K$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $\mathcal{E}(aM)$ is a uniformly integrable martingale for each $a < 1$.

steps.slogan: Let $a$ increase to 1 in the Hölder bound at time infinity.

steps.slogan: Close the supermartingale $\mathcal{E}(M)$ by its limit to get a uniformly integrable martingale.
steps.detail: Fatou gives $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(M)_\infty \le 1$, so the mean is exactly 1. The nonnegative gap $\mathcal{E}(M)_t - \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}(M)_\infty\mid\mathcal{F}_t]$ has mean at most 0 and vanishes.

proofs.name: Inverse clock and Lévy's characterization
proofs.slogan: Run $M$ on the inverse of its own clock $\langle M\rangle$, check that the result is continuous, and recognize a Brownian motion by its martingale properties.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with any initial value $M_0$.

roles.why: The bracket of $M$ exists, and stopped versions of $M$ and $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ are uniformly integrable martingales.
Every level $r$ of the clock is reached, so the [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau_r$ are finite and $\beta$ is defined for all $r$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ stays constant on every interval where its bracket is constant.
steps.detail: For $N_t = M_t - M_{t\wedge a}$, Doob's inequality gives $\mathbb{E}\sup_t N_{t\wedge S^\varepsilon}^2 \le 4\varepsilon$ when $S^\varepsilon$ stops $N$ once its bracket reaches $\varepsilon$. steps.slogan: Prove that the time-changed process $\beta_r = M_{\tau_r}$ is continuous and recovers $M$.
steps.detail: The inverse clock $\tau_r$ jumps only across intervals where $\langle M\rangle$ is flat, and $M$ is constant on those intervals. So $\beta$ has no jumps, and $\tau_{\langle M\rangle_t} \le t \le \tau_{\langle M\rangle_t +}$ gives $M_t = \beta_{\langle M\rangle_t}$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the [martingale](c:martingale) properties of $M$ and $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ to $\beta$ by optional stopping.
steps.detail: Stopped at $\tau_n$, both processes are [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability) martingales because the bracket is at most $n$. Optional stopping at $\tau_r \le \tau_s$ shows that $\beta - \beta_0$ and $(\beta - \beta_0)^2 - r$ are martingales for $\mathcal{F}_{\tau_r}$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\beta$ as a Brownian motion with Lévy's characterization.
steps.detail: The process $\beta$ is a continuous local martingale for the time-changed filtration with bracket $\langle\beta\rangle_r = r$. Lévy's characterization then gives independent Gaussian increments with variance $s - r$.

proofs.slogan: Bound the bracket increments on intervals by a discriminant, extend the bound to all Borel sets, then to all functions.

roles.why: The brackets exist, are continuous and bilinear, and $\langle M+\lambda N\rangle$ is nondecreasing.
Each path of $H$ and $K$ is a Borel function, so the deterministic bound applies path by path.

steps.slogan: Bound each bracket increment by a discriminant of a nonnegative quadratic.
steps.detail: The increment of $\langle M+\lambda N\rangle$ over $(s,t]$ equals $\Delta\langle M\rangle + 2\lambda\Delta\langle M,N\rangle + \lambda^2\Delta\langle N\rangle \ge 0$. A null set that serves all rational $\lambda, s, t$ and continuity give $(\Delta\langle M,N\rangle)^2 \le \Delta\langle M\rangle\,\Delta\langle N\rangle$ for all $s<t$.

steps.slogan: Extend the interval bound to every Borel set by the monotone class theorem.
steps.detail: For finite unions of intervals the bound $|\mu_a(B)| \le (v_1(B)v_2(B))^{1/2}$ follows from Cauchy-Schwarz for sums. The good sets form a monotone class that contains an algebra, so they contain all Borel sets. Summing over partitions gives the same bound for the [total variation](c:bounded-variation) measure of the [signed measure](c:signed-measure) $\mu_a$.

steps.slogan: Pass from indicators to nonnegative Borel functions with simple functions and monotone limits.
steps.detail: For simple $h$ and $k$ on a common partition, Cauchy-Schwarz for sums gives $\int hk\,d|\mu_a| \le (\int h^2dv_1)^{1/2}(\int k^2dv_2)^{1/2}$. Monotone convergence extends this to nonnegative Borel $h$ and $k$ and then from $(0,T]$ to $(0,\infty)$.

steps.slogan: Apply the deterministic bound to the paths of $H$ and $K$ for each good outcome.
steps.detail: Outside the null set of the first step, the paths $|H(\omega)|$ and $|K(\omega)|$ are nonnegative Borel functions, so the function bound applies to them. The signed integral is at most the integral against the total variation measure.

statement: For a continuous [martingale](c:martingale) $M$ bounded in $L^2$ with $M_0 = 0$ and a progressive $H$ with $\mathbb{E}\int_0^\infty H_s^2\,d\langle M\rangle_s < \infty$, the [stochastic integral](c:stochastic-integral) $H\cdot M$ is defined by a linear [isometry](c:isometry), and $\mathbb{E}[(H\cdot M)_\infty^2] = \mathbb{E}\int_0^\infty H_s^2\,d\langle M\rangle_s$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a continuous [martingale](c:martingale) with $M_0 = 0$ and $\sup_t \mathbb{E} M_t^2 < \infty$, for a [filtration](c:filtration) with the usual conditions.
$H$ is progressively measurable and $\mathbb{E}\int_0^\infty H_s^2\,d\langle M\rangle_s < \infty$, where $\langle M\rangle$ is the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) of $M$.

conclusion: The map $H \mapsto H\cdot M$ from elementary processes extends uniquely to a linear isometry $L^2(M) \to \mathbb{H}^2$, so $\mathbb{E}[(\int_0^\infty H_s\,dM_s)^2] = \mathbb{E}\int_0^\infty H_s^2\,d\langle M\rangle_s$.

proofs.name: Isometry on step processes and extension by density
proofs.slogan: Compute the second moment for step integrands, show that step integrands are dense, and extend into the complete space of martingales.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem.

roles.why: Boundedness in $L^2$ makes $\mathbb{H}^2$ a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and makes $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ a true martingale.
The integrand lies in $L^2(M)$, the space on which the extension is defined.

steps.slogan: Show that continuous $L^2$-bounded martingales form a complete space.
steps.detail: A Cauchy sequence has terminal values that converge in $L^2$ to some $Z$. Doob's inequality gives a subsequence that converges uniformly in time almost surely, and the limit equals $\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{F}_t]$, a continuous martingale bounded in $L^2$. So $\mathbb{H}^2$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).

steps.slogan: Compute the second moment of the integral of a step process by conditioning.
steps.detail: Cross terms vanish because each later increment of $M$ has conditional mean zero. Each diagonal term gives $\mathbb{E}[H_{(i)}^2(\langle M\rangle_{t_{i+1}} - \langle M\rangle_{t_i})]$ because $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ is a true martingale. The sum is $\mathbb{E}\int H^2\,d\langle M\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Prove that step processes are [dense](c:dense-set) by showing their orthogonal complement is zero.
steps.detail: If $K$ is orthogonal to all step processes, then $X_t = \int_0^t K\,d\langle M\rangle$ is a continuous martingale of integrable variation. Such a martingale is zero, because its squared increments sum to at most its variation times the largest increment. So $K = 0$ in $L^2(M)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the isometry from step processes to all of $L^2(M)$ by uniform continuity.
steps.detail: Approximate $H$ by step processes. Their integrals form a Cauchy sequence in the complete space $\mathbb{H}^2$, the limit does not depend on the sequence, and the norm identity passes to the limit. Uniqueness holds because the step processes are dense.

concepts.c:martingale: The integrator is a continuous martingale bounded in $L^2$, and so is the integral.
concepts.c:stochastic-integral: The theorem constructs the stochastic integral as the extension of an isometry.
concepts.c:isometry: The integral map preserves the $L^2$ norm, which makes the extension unique.
concepts.c:filtration: The integrand and the integrator are adapted to one filtration with the usual conditions.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The quadratic variation of $M$ is the measure that defines the norm of $L^2(M)$.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Completeness of $\mathbb{H}^2$ gives the limit of the approximating integrals.
concepts.c:dense-set: Density of step processes lets one isometry extend to all integrands.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) with $X_0 = 0$ and [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) $\langle X\rangle$.

conclusion: $Z = \exp(X - \frac12\langle X\rangle)$ solves $dZ = Z\,dX$ with $Z_0 = 1$, every continuous solution equals $Z$, and $Z$ is a local martingale when $X$ is one.

proofs.name: Itô's formula for the candidate and for its inverse
proofs.slogan: Itô's formula shows that $e^{X - \langle X\rangle/2}$ solves the equation, and the product with its inverse shows that no other solution exists.
proofs.scope: The continuous case.

roles.why: Itô's formula needs a continuous semimartingale, and the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) of $X$ gives the second-order term that the $-\frac12\langle X\rangle$ cancels.

steps.slogan: Apply Itô's formula to $F(x,v) = e^{x - v/2}$ at $(X, \langle X\rangle)$.
steps.detail: The $dv$ term $-\frac12 Z\,d\langle X\rangle$ cancels the second-order term $+\frac12 Z\,d\langle X\rangle$, so $dZ = Z\,dX$ and $Z_0 = 1$.

steps.slogan: A stochastic integral against a local martingale is a local martingale.
steps.detail: If $X$ is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale), then $Z = 1 + \int Z\,dX$ is a [stochastic integral](c:stochastic-integral) of a continuous adapted process, so it is a local martingale by localization.

steps.slogan: Compute the differential of the inverse $U = 1/Z$ with Itô's formula.
steps.detail: With $G(x,v) = e^{-x + v/2}$ Itô's formula gives $dU = -U\,dX + U\,d\langle X\rangle$, a drift term that will cancel the covariation.

steps.slogan: Show that the product of any solution $Y$ with $U$ is constant.
steps.detail: The product rule gives $d(YU) = Y\,dU + U\,dY + d\langle Y,U\rangle$, and $d\langle Y,U\rangle = -YU\,d\langle X\rangle$. All four terms cancel, so $YU \equiv 1$.

steps.slogan: Conclude existence, uniqueness and the local martingale property.
steps.detail: From $YU \equiv 1$ we get $Y = 1/U = Z$ for all times almost surely, so the solution is unique and equals the [stochastic exponential](c:stochastic-exponential).

concepts.c:local-martingale: The solution is a local martingale when the driver is a local martingale.

statement: For a linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ and a level $a$, almost surely $|B_t - a| = |B_0 - a| + \int_0^t \operatorname{sgn}(B_s - a)\,dB_s + L^a_t$ for all $t$, where the [local time](c:local-time) $L^a_t = \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0} \frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\int_0^t 1\{|B_s - a| < \varepsilon\}\,ds$ is continuous and nondecreasing.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B_0 = x$, and $a \in \mathbb{R}$ is a fixed level.

conclusion: $|B_t - a| - |B_0 - a| - \int_0^t \operatorname{sgn}(B_s - a)\,dB_s$ is the local time $L^a_t$, a continuous nondecreasing process that grows only when $B = a$.

proofs.name: Itô's formula for a C¹ rounding of the absolute value
proofs.slogan: Round off the corner of $|y - a|$ at scale $\varepsilon$, apply Itô's formula, and let $\varepsilon \to 0$ with Doob's inequality and the isometry.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for a fixed level $a$.

roles.why: Brownian motion has normal marginals, so it spends zero [Lebesgue](c:lebesgue-measure) time at each level, and its [Itô integrals](c:ito-integral) satisfy the isometry with $d\langle B\rangle_s = ds$.

steps.slogan: Brownian motion spends zero Lebesgue time at any fixed level.
steps.detail: By Fubini, $\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{Leb}\{s \le T : B_s = c\} = \int_0^T P(B_s = c)\,ds = 0$, because $B_s$ has a density for $s > 0$.

steps.slogan: Replace the corner of $|y - a|$ by a parabola on $(a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon)$.
steps.detail: The function $f_\varepsilon$ is $C^1$, within $\varepsilon/2$ of $|y - a|$, its derivative differs from $\operatorname{sgn}(y - a)$ only near $a$, and its second derivative is $\frac1\varepsilon 1\{|y - a| < \varepsilon\}$.

steps.slogan: Itô's formula for $f_\varepsilon$ produces the occupation time near $a$.
steps.detail: Mollify $f_\varepsilon$, apply Itô's formula, and pass to the limit with Doob's inequality and dominated convergence. The second-order term becomes $\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\int_0^t 1\{|B_s - a| < \varepsilon\}\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon \to 0$: the error integral is controlled by the time spent near $a$.
steps.detail: Doob and the isometry bound $\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\le T}|L^{a,\varepsilon}_t - L^a_t|^2$ by $2\varepsilon^2 + 8\,\mathbb{E}\int_0^T 1\{|B_s - a| < \varepsilon\}\,ds$, which tends to 0 by the zero-time step.

steps.slogan: Pass monotonicity and support to the [local time](c:local-time) along an almost surely convergent subsequence.
steps.detail: Borel–Cantelli gives $\varepsilon_k$ with uniform convergence on compacts almost surely. Each approximation is nondecreasing and constant on intervals where $B$ stays away from $a$, and the limit keeps both properties.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: The formula is a statement about one-dimensional Brownian motion.
concepts.c:local-time: The correction term in the formula is the local time of $B$ at level $a$.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The martingale part of $|B_t - a|$ is the Itô integral of $\operatorname{sgn}(B_s - a)$.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The local time measures, per unit of space, the Lebesgue time that $B$ spends near $a$.

new_concepts.name: local time
new_concepts.reminder: The local time $L_t^x$ measures how much time a process spends near the level $x$ up to time $t$.
new_concepts.definition: For a one-dimensional [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, the local time is the jointly continuous process $(L_t^x)_{t\ge0,x\in\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\int_0^tf(B_s)\,ds=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)L_t^x\,dx$ for all bounded Borel functions $f$ and all $t$, almost surely. So $x\mapsto L_t^x$ is the [Radon–Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) of the occupation measure $A\mapsto\int_0^t1_A(B_s)\,ds$ with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). For a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$, the same formula with $d\langle X\rangle_s$ in place of $ds$ defines $L_t^x$, which is then right-continuous in $x$.

statement: For a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ with running maximum $M$ and [local time](c:local-time) $L$ at $0$, the [processes](c:stochastic-process) $(M - B, M)$ and $(|B|, L)$ have the same [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution).

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B(0) = 0$.

$L$ is the [local time](c:local-time) of $B$ at $0$ in Tanaka's formula $|B(t)| = \int_0^t \operatorname{sign}(B(s))\,dB(s) + L(t)$, with $L(t) = \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}(2\varepsilon)^{-1}\,\mathrm{Leb}\{s \le t : |B(s)| \le \varepsilon\}$.

conclusion: $((M(t) - B(t), M(t)))_{t\ge 0}$ and $((|B(t)|, L(t)))_{t\ge 0}$ have the same law on $C([0,\infty), \mathbb{R}^2)$.

proofs.name: Tanaka's formula and the reflection argument
proofs.slogan: Tanaka's formula writes $|B| = L - \tilde W$ for a Brownian motion $\tilde W$, and $L$ is exactly the running maximum of $\tilde W$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem.

roles.why: Brownian motion makes $W = \int \operatorname{sign}(B)\,dB$ a continuous martingale with quadratic variation $t$, and the law of $\Phi(B)$ is the target law.
Tanaka's formula links $L$ to $|B|$, and the occupation density shows that $L$ grows only on the zero set.

steps.slogan: Write $|B| = W + L$ with Tanaka's formula, where $W$ is a stochastic integral.
steps.detail: Tanaka's formula at level $0$ gives $|B(t)| = W(t) + L(t)$ for all $t$, where $W(t) = \int_0^t \operatorname{sign}(B(s))\,dB(s)$ is an [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) of a bounded adapted integrand.

steps.slogan: Show that $W$ is a Brownian motion through its quadratic variation and Lévy's characterization.
steps.detail: The [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) is $\langle W\rangle_t = t - \mathrm{Leb}\{s \le t : B(s) = 0\}$, and Tonelli's theorem shows that the zero set has [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $0$. So $\langle W\rangle_t = t$, and $W$ and $\tilde W = -W$ are standard Brownian motions.

steps.slogan: Show that the local time is nondecreasing and grows only on the zero set of $B$.
steps.detail: For rational $s < t$ the increment $L(t) - L(s)$ is the limit of $(2\varepsilon)^{-1}$ times the time spent in $[-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]$ during $[s,t]$. It is nonnegative, and it is zero when $B$ has no zero on $[s,t]$. Continuity extends this to all intervals.

steps.slogan: Identify $L$ with the running maximum of $\tilde W$ by a two-sided comparison.
steps.detail: From $\tilde W = L - |B| \le L$ we get $\max_{s \le t}\tilde W(s) \le L(t)$. At the last zero $s^*$ of $B$ before $t$, $L(t) = L(s^*) = \tilde W(s^*) \le \max_{s\le t}\tilde W(s)$. So $L = \tilde M$ and $|B| = \tilde M - \tilde W$ pathwise.

steps.slogan: Transfer the pathwise identity to an identity in law with a continuous path map.
steps.detail: The map $\Phi(w) = (\max w - w, \max w)$ is continuous on path space. Since $(|B|, L) = \Phi(\tilde W)$ and $\tilde W$ has the law of $B$, the pair has the law of $\Phi(B) = (M - B, M)$.

concepts.c:local-time: The local time at 0 is one coordinate of the identity.
concepts.c:stochastic-process: The identity holds for whole processes, not only at fixed times.
concepts.c:joint-distribution: The two coordinates are compared jointly, as one two-dimensional law.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The process W is the Itô integral of sign(B) against B.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: Quadratic variation t identifies W as a Brownian motion.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The zero set of B has Lebesgue measure zero, so sign(B)² = 1 almost everywhere.

statement: For a [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) with continuous coefficients and a weak solution, [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness) holds if and only if the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of the solution and the [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) is unique and a [strong solution](c:strong-solution) exists.

hypotheses.text: The drift $b(t,x)$ and the diffusion matrix $\sigma(t,x)$ are continuous.
Some filtered probability space carries a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $W$ and a continuous adapted solution $X$ with $X_0$ of law $\mu$.

conclusion: Pathwise uniqueness is equivalent to uniqueness of the law of $(X, W)$ together with $X = F(X_0, W)$ for a Borel map $F$. Then every solution is $F(X_0, W)$ and is adapted to the filtration of $(X_0, W)$.

proofs.name: Randomized solutions coupled on one space
proofs.slogan: Write each solution law as a function of the noise and an independent uniform variable, put two of them on one space, and let pathwise uniqueness merge them.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 3.14 in Kurtz (2007), pp. 959-960, for stochastic differential equations as in Example 3.9.

roles.why: Continuous coefficients make the integrals limits of Riemann sums, so being a solution is a condition on the joint law of $(X, X_0, W)$.
A weak solution gives a solution law to randomize, so the set of solution laws is not empty.

steps.slogan: Recast a solution as a joint law of $(X, Y)$ with $Y = (X_0, W)$ and a compatibility condition.
steps.detail: The equation becomes limit conditions on the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of $(X, Y)$, and compatibility means that $W(t+\cdot)-W(t)$ is independent of the past of $(X, W)$. The set of solution laws is convex (Lemmas 3.2 and 3.8 of the source).

steps.slogan: Represent a solution law as $(F(Y,\xi), Y)$ with an independent uniform variable $\xi$.
steps.detail: Disintegration gives a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) $\eta(y,dx)$ with $\hat\mu(dx\,dy) = \eta(y,dx)\nu(dy)$, and a Borel sampling map $H$ turns a [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) $\xi$ into a variable of law $\eta(y,\cdot)$ (Lemmas 2.2 and A.1).

steps.slogan: Put two randomized solutions on one space with the same noise and prove joint compatibility.
steps.detail: With $Y, \xi_1, \xi_2$ independent, $X_1 = F_{\hat\mu}(Y,\xi_1)$ and $X_2 = F_{\hat\gamma}(Y,\xi_2)$ satisfy $E[f(Y) \mid \mathcal F_t^{X_1} \vee \mathcal F_t^{X_2} \vee \mathcal F_t^Y] = E[f(Y) \mid \mathcal F_t^Y]$ by Lemma 3.7 and a chain of [conditional expectations](c:conditional-expectation).

steps.slogan: Pathwise uniqueness merges the two solutions, which gives one law and a strong solution.
steps.detail: From $X_1 = X_2$ almost surely the two laws agree. Lemma A.2 shows that a function of $(Y, \xi_1)$ that equals a function of $(Y, \xi_2)$ is a function $F(Y)$ of $Y$ alone.

steps.slogan: Show that the [strong solution](c:strong-solution) $F(X_0, W)$ is adapted and solves the equation on every space.
steps.detail: Lemma 3.11 gives $g(X) = E[g(F(Y)) \mid \mathcal F_t^Y]$ for $g$ measurable in the path up to time $t$. So $F(X_0, W)$ is adapted to the noise, and its law is the solution law on any space.

steps.slogan: Derive pathwise uniqueness from a unique law that a strong solution carries.
steps.detail: If the only solution law is the law of $(F(Y), Y)$, its kernel is $\delta_{F(y)}$, so two solutions with the same $Y$ both equal $F(Y)$ almost surely. This gives [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness).

new_concepts.definition: A [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ has pathwise uniqueness when, for any two solutions $X$ and $X'$ on a common filtered probability space with the same [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ and $X_0=X'_0$ almost surely, $P(X_t=X'_t\text{ for all }t\ge0)=1$. new_concepts.name: strong solution of a stochastic differential equation
new_concepts.reminder: A strong solution of a stochastic differential equation is built from the given Brownian motion and initial value alone.
new_concepts.definition: Fix a probability space with a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, an initial value $\xi$ independent of $B$, and the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ that $\xi$ and $B$ generate, augmented by the null sets. A weak solution, in contrast, can use a Brownian motion and a filtration that are constructed together with $X$.

statement: For a one-dimensional [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) with a [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) drift and a diffusion coefficient with modulus $\rho$ such that $\int_0^\gamma \rho(u)^{-2}\,du = \infty$, [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness) holds.

hypotheses.text: The drift satisfies $|b(t,x)-b(t,y)| \le K|x-y|$ for $|x-y| \le \gamma$; it is [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) at small distances.

The diffusion coefficient satisfies $|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)| \le \rho(|x-y|)$ for $|x-y| \le \gamma$, with $\rho$ nondecreasing, positive on $(0,\gamma]$ and $\int_0^\gamma \rho(u)^{-2}\,du = \infty$.
$X$ and $Y$ solve the equation on one probability space with the same [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $W$ and $X_0 = Y_0$ almost surely.

conclusion: $X$ and $Y$ are indistinguishable: almost surely $X_t = Y_t$ for all $t \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Smoothed absolute value and Grönwall's lemma
proofs.slogan: Apply Itô's formula to smooth approximations of $|X-Y|$ whose second derivative is at most $2/(k\rho^2)$, so the noise term costs only $1/k$.
proofs.scope: The full one-dimensional statement.

roles.why: The Lipschitz bound turns the drift term into $K|Z_s|$, which feeds Grönwall's lemma.
The divergent integral gives the levels $a_k$ and the weights $\varphi_k \le 2/(k\rho^2)$ that cancel $\rho^2$ in the Itô correction.
With the same Brownian motion the difference $Z = X - Y$ has a single stochastic integral, and $Z_0 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Build $C^2$ approximations $\psi_k$ of $|w|$ with small second derivative weighted by $\rho^2$.
steps.detail: Choose $a_k \downarrow 0$ with $\int_{a_k}^{a_{k-1}} \rho^{-2} = k$ and a continuous $\varphi_k \le 2/(k\rho^2)$ on $(a_k, a_{k-1})$ with integral 1. Then $\psi_k(w) = \int_0^{|w|}\int_0^v \varphi_k$ satisfies $|\psi_k'| \le 1$, $\psi_k'' = \varphi_k(|w|)$ and $|w| - a_{k-1} \le \psi_k(w) \le |w|$.

steps.slogan: Write the difference $Z = X - Y$ and stop it at the exit [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$.
steps.detail: With $\tau = \inf\{t : |Z_t| \ge \gamma\}$ the hypotheses apply up to $\tau$, so the drift difference is at most $K|Z_s|$ and the diffusion difference at most $\rho(|Z_s|) \le \rho(\gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\psi_k(Z_{t\wedge\tau})$ by Itô's formula and remove the bounded [martingale](c:martingale) part.
steps.detail: Itô's formula gives a stochastic integral with integrand bounded by $\rho(\gamma)$ plus a drift integral with integrand $\psi_k'(Z)\beta + \frac12\varphi_k(|Z|)\alpha^2$. The Itô isometry makes the stochastic integral a martingale with [expected value](c:expected-value) 0.

steps.slogan: Bound the Itô correction by $1/k$ and the drift term by $K|Z_s|$.
steps.detail: Where $\varphi_k(|Z_s|) \ne 0$, the bound $\varphi_k \le 2/(k\rho^2)$ and $\alpha_s^2 \le \rho(|Z_s|)^2$ give $\frac12\varphi_k\alpha_s^2 \le 1/k$. Hence $E\psi_k(Z_{t\wedge\tau}) \le t/k + K\int_0^t E|Z_{s\wedge\tau}|\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Let $k \to \infty$ and close the integral inequality with Grönwall's lemma.
steps.detail: With $u(t) = E|Z_{t\wedge\tau}|$ the bound $\psi_k(w) \ge |w| - a_{k-1}$ gives $u(t) \le a_{k-1} + t/k + K\int_0^t u$. In the limit $u(t) \le K\int_0^t u(s)\,ds$, and Grönwall's lemma gives $u \equiv 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $Z$ never reaches level $\gamma$ and vanishes at all times.
steps.detail: On $\{\tau \le t\}$ the stopped difference has absolute value $\gamma > 0$, so $P(\tau \le t) = 0$ and $Z_t = 0$ almost surely. Rational times and continuity of paths give indistinguishability.

statement: If the coefficients $\sigma$ and $b$ are [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) in space uniformly in time, then the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t = \sigma(t, X_t)\,dB_t + b(t, X_t)\,dt$ has [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness), and for every starting point it has a [strong solution](c:strong-solution).

hypotheses.text: There is $K$ with $\|\sigma(t,x) - \sigma(t,y)\| \le K|x-y|$ and $|b(t,x) - b(t,y)| \le K|x-y|$ for all $t, x, y$, so the coefficients are [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) in space uniformly in time.
The values $\|\sigma(t,0)\|$ and $|b(t,0)|$ are bounded on every interval $[0,T]$.
$B$ is an $m$-dimensional [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with respect to a complete [filtration](c:filtration).

conclusion: Two solutions with the same Brownian motion and equal initial values are indistinguishable, and for each $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ there is a solution with $X_0 = x$, adapted to the filtration of $B$, with $\mathbb{E}\sup_{t \le T}|X_t|^2 < \infty$.

proofs.name: Localization for uniqueness and Picard iteration for existence
proofs.slogan: One maximal $L^2$ estimate gives uniqueness through Grönwall's lemma and a factorial bound for the Picard iterates.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for deterministic initial values $x$ in every dimension.

roles.why: The Lipschitz bound turns differences of coefficients into differences of solutions in the key estimate.
It bounds the coefficients along the constant path $x$, so the first Picard increment has a finite second moment.
The [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) against $B$ is a [martingale](c:martingale) to which Doob's inequality and the Itô isometry apply.

steps.slogan: Bound the stopped maximal distance of two Itô processes by an integral of their mean square distance.
steps.detail: For a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$, Doob's $L^2$ inequality, the Itô isometry and Cauchy-Schwarz give $\mathbb{E}\sup_{s\le t}|\tilde X_{s\wedge\tau} - \tilde Y_{s\wedge\tau}|^2 \le 3\mathbb{E}|\tilde X_0 - \tilde Y_0|^2 + 3(4+t)K^2\int_0^t \mathbb{E}|X_{r\wedge\tau} - Y_{r\wedge\tau}|^2\,dr$.

steps.slogan: Localize two solutions in a ball and close the estimate with Grönwall's lemma.
steps.detail: With $\tau$ the exit time of either solution from the ball of radius $M$, the function $g(t) = \mathbb{E}\sup_{s\le t}|X_{s\wedge\tau} - X'_{s\wedge\tau}|^2$ is bounded and satisfies $g \le C_T\int_0^t g$, so $g = 0$. Letting $M \to \infty$ gives indistinguishability.

steps.slogan: Build Picard iterates and bound their increments by a factorial sequence.
steps.detail: With $X^0 = x$ and $X^{n+1} = x + \int \sigma(s, X^n_s)\,dB_s + \int b(s, X^n_s)\,ds$, the estimate gives $g_{n+1}(t) \le C_T\int_0^t g_n$ for $g_n(t) = \mathbb{E}\sup_{s\le t}|X^n_s - X^{n-1}_s|^2$, hence $g_n(t) \le C'_T C_T^{n-1}t^{n-1}/(n-1)!$.

steps.slogan: Sum the increments to get uniform almost sure and mean square convergence of the iterates.
steps.detail: The square roots of the factorial bounds are summable, so $\sum_n \sup_{t\le T}|X^{n+1}_t - X^n_t|$ has finite mean. The iterates converge uniformly on $[0,T]$ almost surely and in $L^2$ of the supremum norm to a continuous adapted limit $X$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in the recursion to show that the limit is a strong solution.
steps.detail: The Lipschitz bound with Cauchy-Schwarz and the Itô isometry show that both integrals in the recursion converge in $L^2$. So $X$ satisfies the equation for each $t$, then for all $t$ by continuity, and it is a [strong solution](c:strong-solution) of the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation).

statement: If the diffusion matrix $a$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) and positive definite and the drift $b$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function), with linear growth conditions, then the [martingale](c:martingale) problem for the [elliptic operator](c:elliptic-operator) $L_s$ has exactly one solution from every starting point, and the solutions form a [Markov process](c:markov-chain).

hypotheses.text: The diffusion matrix $a(s,x)$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function), symmetric and positive definite, with $|a_{ij}(s,x)| \le C(1+|x|^2)$.
The drift $b(s,x)$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) with $|b_i(s,x)| \le C(1+|x|)$.

conclusion: For every $(s_0, x_0)$ there is exactly one law $P_{s_0,x_0}$ on continuous paths that solves the martingale problem from $(s_0, x_0)$, and $p(s,x,t,A) = P_{s,x}[x(t)\in A]$ is its transition probability.

proofs.name: Localization, Girsanov and perturbation of the heat equation
proofs.slogan: Freeze the continuous diffusion matrix near each point, solve the frozen problem by perturbing the heat equation in $L^p$, and patch the local uniqueness together.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 14.3 in Varadhan's Spring 2011 notes, with Lemmas 14.1 and 14.2.

roles.why: Continuity lets the matrix stay close to a constant near each point, which the perturbation needs, and positive definiteness gives uniform ellipticity on compact sets.
Boundedness on balls lets Girsanov's theorem remove the drift, and linear growth keeps the solution from exploding.

steps.slogan: Solve the parabolic equation for nearly constant $a$ by a Neumann series around the heat equation.
steps.detail: With the heat Green operator $G$ built from the [fundamental solution](c:fundamental-solution) and Jones's bound $\|u_t\|_p + \sum\|u_{ij}\|_p \le C_p\|f\|_p$, the series $u = G(I + \frac12[a-I](G\cdot)_{ij})^{-1}f$ converges when $\sup|a_{ij}-\delta_{ij}|$ is small. It gives $u$ in the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $W^{1,2}_p$ with $\sup|u| \le c(T)\|f\|_p$.

steps.slogan: Identify the occupation integrals of every solution with the PDE solution $u$.
steps.detail: Itô's formula for $u$ gives $E^P\int_{s_0}^T f(t,x(t))\,dt = -u(s_0,x_0)$ for every solution $P$, so the one-dimensional laws agree. Conditional laws of a solution are again solutions, which fixes all finite-dimensional laws.

steps.slogan: Patch local uniqueness along successive exit times into global uniqueness.
steps.detail: Two solutions agree up to the exit [stopping time](c:stopping-time) from a small neighbourhood, because after it both can be continued by the unique local solution. Induction over exit times $\tau_n \to \infty$ gives $P_1 = P_2$ (Lemma 14.1).

steps.slogan: Remove a bounded drift with Girsanov's change of measure.
steps.detail: For uniformly elliptic $a$ and bounded $b$, the density $\exp(\int\langle a^{-1}b, dx\rangle - \frac12\int\langle b, a^{-1}b\rangle ds)$ maps solutions for $[a,0]$ one-to-one onto solutions for $[a,b]$.

steps.slogan: Reduce general coefficients to bounded ones by modifying them outside large balls.
steps.detail: Every solution agrees with the solution for the modified coefficients up to the exit time $\tau_\ell$ from the ball of radius $\ell$, and $\tau_\ell \to \infty$ by continuity of paths. So uniqueness needs no growth condition.

steps.slogan: Prove non-explosion with the Lyapunov function $1+|x|^2$ and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: The growth bounds give $L_s(1+|x|^2) \le C'(1+|x|^2)$, so $E[e^{-C'\tau_\ell}] \le (1+|x_0|^2)/(1+\ell^2)$. The solutions $P^\ell$ then agree on larger and larger events and converge to a solution, which is unique and [Markov](c:markov-chain).
